title: Scaling Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Models via Velocity Matching

paper.title: Scaling Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Models via Velocity Matching
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reward fine-tuning is becoming an important tool for adapting diffusion models to human preferences and task-specific objectives, but existing methods largely inherit policy-gradient machinery from large language models.
Unlike autoregressive models, diffusion models do not provide tractable likelihoods for generated samples. As a result, current approaches either construct trajectory likelihoods from stochastic denoising transitions or approximate endpoint likelihoods with evidence lower bound, introducing additional computation and algorithmic complexity.
We demonstrate that this likelihood-based machinery is not necessary for effective diffusion reward fine-tuning. We propose reward-based velocity matching (RVM), a simple trajectory-free update that acts directly on the velocity field.
RVM reinforces directions associated with high-reward generations, suppresses those with low reward, and involves an optional anchor term controlling drift from a reference velocity.
Notably, it provides a general framework that recovers recent fine-tuning methods, including RAM and DiffusionNFT, as special cases.
Across various large-scale diffusion models reward fine-tuning tasks, RVM is competitive with or outperforms trajectory-based policy-gradient methods under substantially reduced training cost.
We further find that, once the velocity update is simplified, the particular loss variant matters less than reward and anchor design. For video generation, standard preference rewards can favor visually clean but nearly static outputs; introducing a new dynamic-tracking reward that substantially improve motions while improving overall VBench performance. These results suggest that scalable reward fine-tuning for diffusion models is better posed in the native velocity representation than as likelihood-based policy optimization. sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Overview of RVM. Left : RVM fine-tunes Wan2.1-1.3B with a simple reward-weighted velocity-matching loss. Grouped rollouts are scored using public reward models together with our dynamic-tracking (DT) reward, and each generated sample 𝒙 0 i \bm{x}^{i}_{0} is noised once to 𝒙 t i \bm{x}^{i}_{t} and regressed toward its velocity target 𝒗 i = ϵ i − 𝒙 0 i \bm{v}^{i}=\bm{\epsilon}^{i}-\bm{x}^{i}_{0} , with an optional anchor velocity 𝒗 anc \bm{v}_{\mathrm{anc}} controlling model drift, avoiding trajectory storage and likelihood estimation. Right : on Wan2.1-1.3B, RVM achieves the best VBench Overall score at a fraction of the training cost of trajectory-based methods. Diffusion and flow models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2025 ) have become a central class of generative models, achieving strong performance across image, video, and other high-dimensional generation tasks. Reward-based fine-tuning has become an important approach for adapting these models to human preferences ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) and downstream criteria such as semantic alignment, visual quality, motion, and physical plausibility ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Tang et al., 2026 ; Xue et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026b ) . As these models scale, however, efficiency becomes increasingly important because each rewarded sample requires an expensive model rollout. This challenge is particularly pronounced for large-scale models such as video diffusion models, where rollout cost can become a major bottleneck. A dominant approach is to transfer reinforcement-learning (RL) algorithms developed for autoregressive large language models (LLMs), such as PPO and GRPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Shao et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023a ) , to diffusion models. For language models, policy-gradient methods are natural because sequence likelihoods factorize into tractable next-token probabilities. In diffusion models, however, the endpoint likelihood is intractable. Therefore, existing methods recover likelihood-based policy updates indirectly. One line of work, named trajectory-based methods, avoid the intractable final-sample likelihood by using tractable one-step transition probabilities π θ ​ ( 𝒙 t − Δ ​ t ∣ 𝒙 t ) \pi_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t-\Delta t}\mid\bm{x}_{t}) along the sampled denoising trajectory. This is costly, requiring stochastic rollouts and trajectory storage, and can yield high-variance updates because the final reward is assigned through random intermediate transitions. Another line of works approximate the marginal likelihood of the final sample through the evidence lower bound (ELBO) ( Xue et al., 2026a ; Choi et al., 2026 ) . Given a generated sample 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} , the ELBO provides a likelihood surrogate from independently noised states 𝒙 t \bm{x}_{t} , removing reverse-trajectory storage and decoupling training from the rollout sampler, allowing fast deterministic ODE sampling. However, these methods still originate from a likelihood-based policy-gradient formulation and retain an estimated policy ratio. This raises the central question of this work: If the model update produced by an ELBO-based policy gradient already reduces to reward-weighted velocity regression, is likelihood estimation necessary at all? We find that the likelihood perspective is unnecessary for effective reward fine-tuning. Rather than first constructing a policy-gradient objective and then approximating its intractable likelihood ratio, we act directly on the native training representation of the diffusion model. Given generated endpoints 𝒙 0 i \bm{x}_{0}^{i} , we forward-noise each sample to a single intermediate state 𝒙 t i \bm{x}_{t}^{i} with velocity target 𝒗 i \bm{v}^{i} , and use the reward as a signed preference signal for that velocity direction. This gives reward-based velocity matching (RVM), ℒ rvm = 1 2 ​ 𝔼 ​ [ r i ​ ‖ 𝒗 θ ​ ( 𝒙 t i , t ) − 𝒗 i ‖ 2 2 + β ⁡ ( r i ) ​ ‖ 𝒗 θ ​ ( 𝒙 t i , t ) − 𝒗 anc ​ ( 𝒙 t i , t ) ‖ 2 2 ] , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rvm}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\,r^{i}\,\big\|{\bm{v}_{\theta}}(\bm{x}_{t}^{i},t)-\bm{v}^{i}\big\|_{2}^{2}+\beta(r^{i})\,\big\|{\bm{v}_{\theta}}(\bm{x}_{t}^{i},t)-\bm{v}_{\mathrm{anc}}(\bm{x}_{t}^{i},t)\big\|_{2}^{2}\,\Big], where r i r^{i} is a reward-derived weight and 𝒗 anc \bm{v}_{\mathrm{anc}} is an optional anchor velocity. Positive reward weights reinforce the velocity direction associated with a generated sample, while negative weights suppress it. The anchor provides an independent mechanism for controlling model drift and retaining desirable properties of a reference model. Despite its simplicity, RVM generalizes several recent loss functionals, recovering Reinforce Adjoint Matching (RAM) ( Bergmeister et al., 2026 ) and DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al., 2026a ) as special cases under particular choices of reward design and anchor velocity. This unification shifts attention away from the precise algebraic form of the velocity loss and toward the choices that remain: how rewards are transformed into update weights, how the model is anchored, and how samples are generated. We test this view across three generative settings: text-to-image generation with Stable Diffusion 3.5 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , text-to-video generation with Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B ( Team Wan et al., 2025 ) , and image-to-video generation with SkyReels-I2V ( Chen et al., 2025b ) . Across these settings, trajectory-independent velocity-based methods consistently match or outperform trajectory-based baselines. They are also substantially cheaper to train. As demonstrated in Fig. 1 , on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, our RVM recipe uses a 16-step deterministic ODE rollout ( Zhang & Chen, 2023 ; Lu et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023b ) without classifier-free guidance (CFG) and is much efficient, yet achieves higher performance at much lower training cost than trajectory-based methods such as DanceGRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) and FlowGRPO ( Liu et al., 2025b ) . Our experiments on video models further reveal reward design as a key factor. Standard preference and visual-quality rewards can improve even as generated videos become nearly static. To address this failure mode, we introduce a dynamic-tracking (DT) reward based on optical flow that explicitly encourages meaningful motion. Adding DT alone substantially improves VBench Dynamic Degree while also increasing the overall VBench score. These results suggest that reward specification, rather than increasingly elaborate policy-loss design, may be the more influential choices for scalable diffusion-model post-training. Our main contributions are: • We introduce RVM, a simple trajectory-independent method that incorporates reward feedback directly into the native velocity-matching representation of a diffusion model, avoiding policy-ratio estimation and trajectory storage. • We show that RVM provides a general framework that recovers recent methods, including RAM and DiffusionNFT, as special cases. • Through extensive experiments, we show that velocity-based methods can substantially reduce training cost while matching or improving generation quality. Moreover, the differences among velocity-loss variants are relatively small compared with the effects of reward and anchor design. • We extend this framework to large-scale video diffusion models and identify a tendency of generic preference rewards to favor static videos and introduce a dynamic-tracking reward that substantially improves motion while preserving overall video quality.

sections.heading: Trajectory-based approaches.
sections.text: For diffusion and flow models, the marginal likelihood π θ ​ ( 𝒙 0 ) \pi_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{0}) of a generated sample is intractable ( Song et al., 2020 ; Benton et al., 2024 ) , so the policy ratio ρ θ ​ ( 𝒙 0 ) \rho_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{0}) in GRPO cannot be formed directly. Trajectory-based methods address this difficulty by replacing the intractable marginal log-likelihood log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝒙 0 ) \log\pi_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{0}) with the tractable per-step Gaussian transition log-likelihood log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝒙 t − Δ ​ t ∣ 𝒙 t ) \log\pi_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t-\Delta t}\mid\bm{x}_{t}) , the current policy is updated at each denoising step through the Gaussian transitions induced by an SDE sampler ( Black et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2023 ) . FlowGRPO ( Liu et al., 2025b ) clips these per-step ratios individually, and DanceGRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) carries the recipe over to video, both at the cost of simulating the full trajectory under CFG. Moreover, tying the objective to per-step transition likelihoods makes the update dependent on the particular SDE sampler used during training. It can also introduce additional variance, since the next denoising state 𝒙 t − Δ ​ t \bm{x}_{t-\Delta t} is itself a stochastic intermediate sample and need not be closer to the clean endpoint 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} than the current state 𝒙 t \bm{x}_{t} .

sections.heading: 3 Designing Simple and Efficient Diffusion Fine-tuning
sections.text: In this section, we present a simple velocity-matching recipe for reward fine-tuning of video diffusion models. In Sec. 3.1 , we introduce our objective alongside existing velocity-based losses. In Sec. 3.2 , we show how these losses connect. We then turn to reward shaping in Sec. 4.3 , which our analysis identifies as the factor that governs performance.

sections.heading: Our simplified loss.
sections.text: We propose a simple objective for reward fine-tuning of diffusion models that consists of two velocity-regression terms, without using policy ratios or assigning a likelihood interpretation to the loss. The first term performs reward-weighted velocity matching, pulling the predicted velocity toward the velocity directions of high-reward samples. The second term anchors the prediction to an anchor velocity 𝒗 anc \bm{v}_{\mathrm{anc}} , preventing excessive policy drift during fine-tuning. Precisely, we draw a group of samples { 𝒙 0 i } i = 1 G \{\bm{x}^{i}_{0}\}^{G}_{i=1} from a sampling policy π old \pi_{\mathrm{old}} , noise each to a single state 𝒙 t i = ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝒙 0 i + t ​ ϵ i \bm{x}_{t}^{i}=(1-t)\,\bm{x}_{0}^{i}+t\,\bm{\epsilon}^{i} with t ∼ Unif ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) t\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1) , ϵ i ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝑰 ) \bm{\epsilon}^{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}) , and train the current velocity model 𝒗 θ {\bm{v}_{\theta}} with these two regression terms. This gives our reward-weighted velocity matching (RVM) objective: ℒ rvm = 1 2 𝔼 𝒙 1 : G 0 ∼ π old [ r rvm i ∥ 𝒗 θ ( 𝒙 t i , t ) − 𝒗 i ∥ 2 2 + β ( r rvm i ) ∥ 𝒗 θ ( 𝒙 t i , t ) − 𝒗 anc ( 𝒙 t i , t ) ∥ 2 2 ] , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rvm}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\ \mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}^{1:G}_{0}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{old}}}\left[r^{i}_{\mathrm{rvm}}\,\|{\bm{v}_{\theta}}(\bm{x}_{t}^{i},t)-\bm{v}^{i}\|_{2}^{2}+\beta(r^{i}_{\mathrm{rvm}})\,\|{\bm{v}_{\theta}}(\bm{x}_{t}^{i},t)-\bm{v}_{\mathrm{anc}}(\bm{x}_{t}^{i},t)\|_{2}^{2}\right], (RVM) where 𝒗 i := ϵ i − 𝒙 0 i \bm{v}^{i}:=\bm{\epsilon}^{i}-\bm{x}_{0}^{i} and β : ℝ → ℝ \beta:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is an anchor strength function. This objective is governed by two design choices: (I) the reward r rvm i r_{\mathrm{rvm}}^{i} and (II) the anchor velocity 𝒗 anc \bm{v}_{\mathrm{anc}} . The reward r rvm i r_{\mathrm{rvm}}^{i} acts as a signed preference signal for the velocity direction associated with sample 𝒙 0 i \bm{x}_{0}^{i} . When r rvm i > 0 r_{\mathrm{rvm}}^{i}>0 , the sample velocity 𝒗 i \bm{v}^{i} is treated as a desirable direction, and the model is encouraged to match it. When r rvm i < 0 r_{\mathrm{rvm}}^{i}<0 , the same velocity direction is treated as undesirable, and the update discourages the model from following directions that would reproduce such samples. The anchor term provides a reference velocity around which this reward-driven attraction or repulsion is controlled. The anchor velocity 𝒗 anc \bm{v}_{\mathrm{anc}} regularizes the update, keeping 𝒗 θ {\bm{v}_{\theta}} close to a trusted velocity field with strength β \beta . We can use the frozen reference velocity 𝒗 ref \bm{v}_{\mathrm{ref}} or an EMA-updated velocity of the current policy. In Sec. 4.3 , we ablate over various choices of the reward r rvm i r^{i}_{\mathrm{rvm}} and anchor velocity 𝒗 anc \bm{v}_{\mathrm{anc}} .

sections.heading: Efficiency of RVM.
sections.text: As shown in Fig. 2 , trajectory-based losses reinforce the likelihood of the sampled one-step transition π θ ​ ( 𝒙 t − Δ ​ t ∣ 𝒙 t ) \pi_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t-\Delta t}\mid\bm{x}_{t}) , and therefore reinforce the stochastic move from 𝒙 t \bm{x}_{t} to the next denoising state 𝒙 t − Δ ​ t \bm{x}_{t-\Delta t} . Since 𝒙 t − Δ ​ t \bm{x}_{t-\Delta t} is an intermediate state sampled by the SDE solver, this direction can vary across rollouts and need not provide the most direct signal toward the clean endpoint 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} . In contrast, our velocity-matching loss uses the endpoint-defined target 𝒗 i = ϵ i − 𝒙 0 i \bm{v}^{i}=\bm{\epsilon}^{i}-\bm{x}^{i}_{0} , obtained by noising the final sample to a single state. A positive reward encourages the predicted velocity to align with this clean-sample direction, while a negative reward pushes it away from directions associated with undesirable samples. Intuitively, this gives RVM a more direct and potentially lower-variance learning signal than trajectory-based losses.

sections.heading: 3.2 Connection between the Objectives
sections.text: While RAM ( Bergmeister et al., 2026 ) and DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al., 2026a ) are motivated from control-theoretic and contrastive-learning perspectives, respectively, we show that both can be interpreted as special cases of RVM.

Thus, RAM is update-equivalent to on-policy RVM ( π old = π θ \pi_{\mathrm{old}}=\pi_{\theta} ) with the frozen reference as its anchor.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Our experiments address the following two questions: Can reward-based diffusion fine-tuning be simplified to velocity matching without sacrificing performance? And if so, what design choices actually matter? We focus primarily on image and video diffusion models, where each rewarded sample requires an expensive model rollout and training efficiency is particularly desirable. Our main findings are: • In Sec. 4.2 , we compare trajectory-based, ELBO-based, and other recent approaches against our RVM formulation. Our velocity-based approach is comparable or better in both quality and efficiency , achieving comparable or higher reward and benchmark scores with fewer GPU hours. More importantly, we demonstrate that the particular velocity-matching loss forms matter little: RVM, RAM, and DiffusionNFT perform comparably. • In Sec. 4.3 , we isolate the two design choices that remain, (i) the reward and how it is shaped and (ii) the anchoring velocity , and find that the reward function itself is the critical factor . Its choice and the way it is shaped into the per-sample weight account for most of the gain. The choice of anchoring velocity matters in a different way, governing the training dynamics rather than the metrics. A well-chosen anchor keeps the updates faithful and help to gain semantic property.

sections.heading: Base models.
sections.text: We evaluate reward fine-tuning across text-to-image (T2I), text-to-video (T2V), and image-to-video (I2V) models using Stable Diffusion 3.5 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B ( Team Wan et al., 2025 ) , and SkyReels-I2V ( Chen et al., 2025b ) , respectively. All models are fine-tuned with LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) using publicly available prompt sets and reward models. Importantly, we separate the rewards used for training from the metrics used for evaluation, allowing us to assess whether improvements generalize beyond the optimized reward signals.

sections.heading: Default configuration.
sections.text: Unless otherwise stated, we train with RVM following implementation of Choi et al. (2026) . For video models, we use β ≡ c \beta\equiv c where c c is a constant, and sample with a deterministic DPM-Solver-2 ODE ( Lu et al., 2022 ) , using neither CFG nor policy-ratio clipping. The loss is computed directly as velocity regression, and the anchor strength is β = 0 \beta=0 , so each update reduces to the reward-weighted velocity regression alone. At evaluation, we generate one video per prompt. Full hyperparameters are listed in App. C .

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: For T2I diffusion models, we follow the evaluation of Liu et al. (2025b) ; Zheng et al. (2026a) ; Choi et al. (2026) . For video model, we train and evaluate along two axes. First, we report the VideoAlign and HPSv3 reward scores, the same rewards used during training. Second, we report the standardized benchmarks VBench ( Huang et al., 2024 ) for the T2V model and VBench-I2V ( Huang et al., 2026b ) for the I2V models. The Vbench score comprises two parts: Qualtiy and Semantic score. The Overall Vbench score is computed by a weighted sum 0.8 ⋅ Quality + 0.2 ⋅ Semantic 0.8\cdot\text{Quality}+0.2\cdot\text{Semantic} for VBench and the average of the two scores for VBench-I2V.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare against three groups, namely (i) the pretrained base model, evaluated without CFG and with CFG at scale 5 5 using the official negative prompt; (ii) trajectory-based RL methods, FlowGRPO ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , DanceGRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) , and TaRoS ( Li et al., 2026b ) ; and (iii) trajectory-independent velocity-based methods, DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al., 2026a ) , RAM ( Bergmeister et al., 2026 ) , and our RVM. We cite published DanceGRPO and TaRoS numbers, obtained under a different protocol (CFG, a 50-step SDE, five videos per prompt) and therefore uncontrolled.

sections.heading: Velocity matching outperforms trajectory-based fine-tuning.
sections.text: Across both T2V and I2V settings, velocity-matching objectives consistently outperform trajectory-based policy-gradient methods. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, RVM achieves the best VBench Overall score of 84.13 84.13 , improving over FlowGRPO ( 75.91 75.91 ), DanceGRPO ( 79.46 79.46 ), and TaRoS-72B ( 80.56 80.56 ). The gain is especially pronounced in motion: RVM reaches a dynamic degree of 75.00 75.00 , compared to 55 55 – 58 58 for trajectory-based methods. A similar trend appears on SkyReels-I2V, where FlowGRPO degrades the base model from 81.68 81.68 to 77.97 77.97 Overall, while RVM reaches 86.27 86.27 . These results suggest that reward-based video diffusion fine-tuning does not require trajectory-level policy-gradient updates to obtain strong performance.

sections.heading: The specific velocity-matching objective matters little.
sections.text: On both video diffusion models, DiffusionNFT, RAM, and RVM achieve similar performance across both reward metrics and VBench scores, with differences limited to a few points. These performance gaps between velocity-matching methods are small compared to their improvement over the CFG-free base model. This agrees with the analysis in Sec. 3.2 that the three objectives share the same anchored velocity-matching structure, suggesting that the particular loss variant is not the main driver of performance. Furthermore, on the T2I OCR, RVM performs competitively with ELBO-based methods. As shown in Tab. 3 , it achieves the best score on nearly every metric and performs on par with the ELBO-based baseline (PEPG).

sections.heading: Velocity-matching approaches are efficient.
sections.text: Velocity matching substantially reduces training cost because each update uses a single noised state rather than a stored SDE trajectory. As shown in Fig. 5 , our RVM recipe costs 525 525 GPU-hours for a full Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B run on 8 × 8\times H100, compared to 1,159 1{,}159 GPU-hours for FlowGRPO and 6,171 6{,}171 GPU-hours for DanceGRPO/TaRoS. This corresponds to a 2.2 × 2.2\times and 11.8 × 11.8\times reduction, respectively. The gap comes from two sources: trajectory-based methods require more function evaluations per rollout, and they are trained for more iterations under their standard protocols. In particular, RVM uses a 16 16 -step ODE without CFG, FlowGRPO uses a 40 40 -step SDE without CFG, and DanceGRPO/TaRoS use a 50 50 -step SDE with CFG, corresponding to 100 100 function evaluations per video.

sections.heading: 4.3 Further Analysis
sections.text: In this section, we ablate the remaining design choices: the reward formulation and the anchor regularization term.

sections.heading: Ablation on reward settings for video diffusion models.
sections.text: We construct reward signals from publicly available models and combine them through a weighted sum. We study three reward settings. The first uses the VideoAlign ( Liu et al., 2025c ) rewards: text alignment (TA), motion quality (MQ), and visual quality (VQ). The second replaces VQ with HPSv3 ( Ma et al., 2025 ) , a human-preference-based quality reward. However, we find that VideoAlign and HPSv3 alone are not sufficient, as they can still favor visually clean but nearly static videos. To address this, we further add a dynamic-tracking (DT) reward, built on RAFT optical flow ( Teed & Deng, 2020 ) , which explicitly encourages meaningful motion. • VideoAlign : text alignment (TA), motion quality (MQ), and visual quality (VQ). • VideoAlign + HPSv3 : TA, MQ, and HPSv3 (human preference). • VideoAlign + HPSv3 + DT : TA, MQ, HPSv3, and dynamical tracking (DT). The detailed reward design and weights are discussed in Sec. C.3 . Unless otherwise stated, we used the last mixture as our default reward. As shown in Fig. 5 , the DT reward is crucial for improving actual video quality . The DT reward is the main factor behind the improvement in motion. Without DT, dynamic degree remains very low, even after adding HPSv3. Adding DT raises dynamic degree from 5.56 5.56 to 75.00 75.00 and improves VBench Overall from 80.39 80.39 to 84.13 84.13 , showing that explicit motion reward is crucial for effective video fine-tuning.

sections.heading: Few-step generation.
sections.text: We also test whether fine-tuning improves few-step sampling robustness. Starting from the trained 16 16 -step noise grid, we sub-sample it to 5 5 and 4 4 steps while keeping the same low-noise tail, and evaluate the same checkpoints under each schedule using the official 16-dimensional VBench aggregation with one video per prompt. As shown in Fig. 7 , the base model degrades sharply as the number of steps decreases, even with CFG at guidance scale 5 5 : VBench Total drops from 83.10 83.10 at 16 16 steps to 73.62 73.62 at 5 5 steps and 64.39 64.39 at 4 4 steps. In contrast, CFG-free RVM is much more stable, losing only 0.43 0.43 points at 5 5 steps and 1.83 1.83 points at 4 4 steps; notably, its 4 4 -step samples remain comparable to the 16 16 -step base model with CFG. This suggests that RVM does more than improve reward scores: by directly matching velocities toward rewarded clean samples 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} , it learns a velocity field with less curvature towards high-reward samples, making the sampler robust even under aggressive step reduction.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we developed reward-based velocity matching (RVM), a simple trajectory-free loss for reward fine-tuning diffusion models, and showed that it unifies recent velocity-based objectives such as RAM and DiffusionNFT at the level of velocity-field updates. Our experiments verify that these velocity-matching losses are scalable and effective even for video fine-tuning, where each rollout is expensive. More importantly, we find that the specific loss functional matters less than the reward design: carefully shaped rewards are crucial for translating reward optimization into actual improvements in motion and visual quality. A natural future direction is to extend this framework to autoregressive video generation.

sections.heading: Impact Statement
sections.text: This paper presents work aimed at advancing the field of generative models. It proposes a simple approach to reward fine-tuning of video diffusion models. For example, it may be abused to create various harmful and offensive content. We strongly caution the community against such use cases.

sections.heading: RL fine-tuning for language models
sections.text: RL has been extensively studied as a principled approach for improving language-model capabilities and alignment ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . Popular methods include PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , and their variants ( Liu et al., 2025d ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) . Recent algorithmic developments focus on designing more stable policy objectives ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025b ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Kimi Team et al., 2025 ) and understanding their estimation and optimization behavior ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2025a ; Liu et al., 2025a ) . QUATRO ( Lee et al., 2026a ) is closely related to our policy-gradient formulation, as it studies proximal sequence-level policy optimization for likelihood-based LLMs. However, directly transferring these methods to diffusion and flow models is nontrivial because diffusion-model likelihoods and likelihood ratios are intractable.

sections.heading: Trajectory-based RL for diffusion and flow models
sections.text: RL has also been widely adopted to fine-tune diffusion and flow models toward human preferences or task-specific rewards ( Fan et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ) . A dominant line of work follows a trajectory-based view, where the denoising or flow trajectory is treated as the policy trajectory. FlowGRPO ( Liu et al., 2025b ) adapts GRPO to diffusion models using trajectory-based likelihood estimation and achieves strong results in text-to-image generation. Subsequent works improve this recipe through better trajectory estimators, samplers, or rollout structures ( He et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Xue et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Ye et al., 2025 ; Xue et al., 2026a ) . Other examples include MixGRPO ( Li et al., 2026a ) , BranchGRPO ( Li et al., 2026c ) , and LeapAlign ( Liang et al., 2026 ) , which modify the rollout or trajectory construction. Reward Score Matching ( Lee et al., 2026b ) unifies many of these trajectory-based methods as score-matching regressions toward a value-guided target, and can be viewed as a trajectory-level counterpart of the ELBO-based approaches ( EPG ). While effective, these methods are often coupled to the sampling trajectory and can incur substantial memory and compute overhead, especially for video generation.

sections.heading: Simplified and trajectory-independent diffusion fine-tuning
sections.text: A separate line of work seeks simpler alternatives that avoid explicit trajectory-level likelihood estimation. DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al., 2026a ) adapts negative fine-tuning ( Chen et al., 2026 ) to diffusion and flow models by directly modifying velocity-regression losses. AWM ( Xue et al., 2026a ) and RAM ( Bergmeister et al., 2026 ) similarly replace trajectory-based policy-gradient estimation with simpler velocity- or score-based objectives. Relatedly, DPPO ( Ren et al., 2025 ) applies PPO-style updates to diffusion policies in continuous-control and robotic-manipulation settings, while Q-score matching ( Psenka et al., 2024 ) learns diffusion policies from reward signals by matching score functions with Q-function gradients. Choi et al. (2026) shows that, for diffusion fine-tuning, simple objectives can perform competitively when the likelihood or velocity-based training loss is chosen carefully. Our work follows this direction, focusing on trajectory-independent velocity-based losses and analyzing when objective engineering is actually necessary. Concurrently, Xu et al. (2026) present a unified path-space view in which reverse-trajectory and forward-matching methods arise from a common importance-sampling-based policy-gradient principle, attributing empirical gaps between method families to variance reduction rather than differing RL principles. Their unification operates on trajectory-space likelihood ratios, whereas RVM unifies velocity-based methods directly in the model’s native velocity representation, avoiding likelihood estimation altogether.

sections.heading: RL fine-tuning for video diffusion models
sections.text: Recent works have begun to apply RL-style fine-tuning to video diffusion and autoregressive video generators. DanceGRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) and FlowGRPO-based video extensions apply GRPO-style objectives to video generation, while KVPO ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , RAVEN ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , TAGRPO ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , SAGE-GRPO ( Zheng et al., 2026b ) , AR-CoPO ( He et al., 2026a ) , V-GRPO ( Tang et al., 2026 ) , and recent systematic video fine-tuning frameworks ( Xue et al., 2026b ) explore different objectives, rollout strategies, and video-specific reward designs. Other works focus on reward construction, including TaRoS ( Li et al., 2026b ) , Adv-GRPO ( Mao et al., 2025 ) , Diffusion-DRF ( Wang et al., 2026c ) , AlphaGRPO ( Huang et al., 2026a ) , and PromptRL ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . In contrast to recipes that combine clipping, CFG, trajectory-based losses, and reward engineering simultaneously, our work isolates the key components and shows that simple trajectory-independent velocity-based training, combined with careful reward design, is sufficient for efficient and stable video diffusion fine-tuning.

sections.text: RVM RVM is the velocity-regression form we optimize, a reward-weighted velocity regression r rvm i ​ ‖ 𝒗 θ ​ ( 𝒙 t i , t ) − 𝒗 i ‖ 2 2 r^{i}_{\mathrm{rvm}}\,\|{\bm{v}_{\theta}}(\bm{x}_{t}^{i},t)-\bm{v}^{i}\|_{2}^{2} where the reward acts as a signed coefficient on the endpoint-defined velocity target. sections.text: RAM RAM dispenses with the likelihood ratio entirely and instead shapes the velocity-regression target. sections.heading: C.1 Experiment Setup
sections.text: We fine-tune each base model with LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. Fine-tuning is classifier-free-guidance-free: samples are drawn with a deterministic 16 16 -step DPM-Solver-2 flow ODE ( Lu et al., 2022 ) at guidance scale 1.0 1.0 , and the loss is computed as reward-weighted velocity regression at a single noised state per generation, with no policy-ratio clipping. We optimize with AdamW ( β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}{=}0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}{=}0.999 , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon{=}10^{-8} ) at learning rate 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} in bf16, with gradient clipping at norm 1.0 1.0 and a fixed seed. Each iteration draws a group of K = 8 K{=}8 samples for each of N N prompts. The default RVM run uses no anchor ( β = 0 \beta{=}0 ), so each update is the reward-weighted velocity regression alone; an exponential-moving-average copy of the policy (decay 0.9 0.9 ) is maintained and serves as the EMA anchor in the anchor ablation of Sec. 4.3 . Per-model settings are listed in Tab. 5 .

sections.heading: Training and evaluation data
sections.text: Both video models are trained on publicly available prompt sets. For Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, we use the prompt corpus released by DanceGRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) , derived from VidProM ( Wang & Yang, 2024 ) , consisting of 48,998 48{,}998 training prompts, which we use as released without further preprocessing. For SkyReels-I2V, we follow the image-to-video protocol of DanceGRPO and train on 27,000 27{,}000 prompts constructed from ConsisID ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) ; since the model conditions on a reference first frame, we pre-generate one reference image per prompt with FLUX ( Labs, 2024 ) at the model’s native 640 × 400 640\times 400 geometry and cache the resulting prompt–image pairs before training. For evaluation, Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B generates one video per prompt from the extended rewrites of the 946 946 -prompt VBench suite released by Self Forcing ( Huang et al., 2025 ) and is scored with the official VBench protocol ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , while SkyReels-I2V uses the official VBench-I2V suite ( Huang et al., 2026b ) of 1,118 1{,}118 prompt–reference-image pairs, whose reference images match the same native geometry.

sections.heading: Few-step Evaluation
sections.text: For the few-step evaluation of Sec. 4.3 , we sub-sample the trained 16 16 -step noise grid to the noise levels ( 0.999 , 0.889 , 0.727 , 0.348 ) (0.999,\,0.889,\,0.727,\,0.348) for 4 4 steps and ( 0.999 , 0.960 , 0.889 , 0.727 , 0.348 ) (0.999,\,0.960,\,0.889,\,0.727,\,0.348) for 5 5 steps, each followed by the terminal level 0 0 , so both schedules keep the same low-noise tail. sections.text: Training is CFG-free throughout: samples are drawn with a deterministic 10 10 -step DPM-Solver-2 flow ODE at guidance scale 1.0 1.0 , and the same guidance scale is used for the training and reference velocities. Each epoch draws 48 48 prompts from the OCR prompt set with a group of K = 24 K{=}24 images per prompt, followed by a single gradient update over the accumulated batch. We optimize with AdamW at learning rate 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} with gradient clipping at norm 0.02 0.02 , use the adaptive ELBO weighting w ⁡ ( t ) w(t) ( Sec. B.3 ), and train for 500 500 epochs on 6 × 6\times H100 GPUs ( ∼ 41 {\sim}41 hours). The per-sample reward weight is the mean-subtracted reward within each prompt group, and the anchor term uses the frozen reference velocity with strength β = 10 − 4 \beta=10^{-4} . The full settings are collected in Tab. 5 .

sections.heading: Reward
sections.text: The training reward is an equal-weight sum of four components: an OCR accuracy reward computed by PaddleOCR on the rendered text, PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) (rescaled by 1 / 26 1/26 inside the scorer), CLIPScore ( Hessel et al., 2021 ) , and HPSv2.1 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) .

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: Evaluation follows Choi et al. (2026) : images are sampled with 40 40 steps, and we report OCR accuracy together with the held-out preference metrics PickScore, ClipScore, HPSv2.1, Aesthetic score, and ImageReward in Tab. 3 .

Unlike autoregressive models, diffusion models do not provide tractable likelihoods for generated samples. As a result, current approaches either construct trajectory likelihoods from stochastic denoising transitions or approximate endpoint likelihoods with evidence lower bound, introducing additional computation and algorithmic complexity. We demonstrate that this likelihood-based machinery is not necessary for effective diffusion reward fine-tuning. We propose reward-based velocity matching (RVM), a simple trajectory-free update that acts directly on the velocity field. RVM reinforces directions associated with high-reward generations, suppresses those with low reward, and involves an optional anchor term controlling drift from a reference velocity. Notably, it provides a general framework that recovers recent fine-tuning methods, including RAM and DiffusionNFT, as special cases. Across various large-scale diffusion models reward fine-tuning tasks, RVM is competitive with or outperforms trajectory-based policy-gradient methods under substantially reduced training cost. We further find that, once the velocity update is simplified, the particular loss variant matters less than reward and anchor design. For video generation, standard preference rewards can favor visually clean but nearly static outputs; introducing a new dynamic-tracking reward that substantially improve motions while improving overall VBench performance. These results suggest that scalable reward fine-tuning for diffusion models is better posed in the native velocity representation than as likelihood-based policy optimization. Project page : https://jaemoo-choi.github.io/RVM/ 1 Introduction Figure 1: Overview of RVM. Left : RVM fine-tunes Wan2.1-1.3B with a simple reward-weighted velocity-matching loss. Grouped rollouts are scored using public reward models together with our dynamic-tracking (DT) reward, and each generated sample 𝒙 0 i \bm{x}^{i}_{0} is noised once to 𝒙 t i \bm{x}^{i}_{t} and regressed toward its velocity target 𝒗 i = ϵ i − 𝒙 0 i \bm{v}^{i}=\bm{\epsilon}^{i}-\bm{x}^{i}_{0} , with an optional anchor velocity 𝒗 anc \bm{v}_{\mathrm{anc}} controlling model drift, avoiding trajectory storage and likelihood estimation. Right : on Wan2.1-1.3B, RVM achieves the best VBench Overall score at a fraction of the training cost of trajectory-based methods. Diffusion and flow models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2025 ) have become a central class of generative models, achieving strong performance across image, video, and other high-dimensional generation tasks. Reward-based fine-tuning has become an important approach for adapting these models to human preferences ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) and downstream criteria such as semantic alignment, visual quality, motion, and physical plausibility ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Tang et al., 2026 ; Xue et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026b ) . As these models scale, however, efficiency becomes increasingly important because each rewarded sample requires an expensive model rollout. This challenge is particularly pronounced for large-scale models such as video diffusion models, where rollout cost can become a major bottleneck. A dominant approach is to transfer reinforcement-learning (RL) algorithms developed for autoregressive large language models (LLMs), such as PPO and GRPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Shao et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023a ) , to diffusion models. For language models, policy-gradient methods are natural because sequence likelihoods factorize into tractable next-token probabilities. In diffusion models, however, the endpoint likelihood is intractable. Therefore, existing methods recover likelihood-based policy updates indirectly. One line of work, named trajectory-based methods, avoid the intractable final-sample likelihood by using tractable one-step transition probabilities π θ ​ ( 𝒙 t − Δ ​ t ∣ 𝒙 t ) \pi_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t-\Delta t}\mid\bm{x}_{t}) along the sampled denoising trajectory. This is costly, requiring stochastic rollouts and trajectory storage, and can yield high-variance updates because the final reward is assigned through random intermediate transitions. Another line of works approximate the marginal likelihood of the final sample through the evidence lower bound (ELBO) ( Xue et al., 2026a ; Choi et al., 2026 ) . Given a generated sample 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} , the ELBO provides a likelihood surrogate from independently noised states 𝒙 t \bm{x}_{t} , removing reverse-trajectory storage and decoupling training from the rollout sampler, allowing fast deterministic ODE sampling. However, these methods still originate from a likelihood-based policy-gradient formulation and retain an estimated policy ratio. This raises the central question of this work: If the model update produced by an ELBO-based policy gradient already reduces to reward-weighted velocity regression, is likelihood estimation necessary at all? We find that the likelihood perspective is unnecessary for effective reward fine-tuning. Rather than first constructing a policy-gradient objective and then approximating its intractable likelihood ratio, we act directly on the native training representation of the diffusion model. Given generated endpoints 𝒙 0 i \bm{x}_{0}^{i} , we forward-noise each sample to a single intermediate state 𝒙 t i \bm{x}_{t}^{i} with velocity target 𝒗 i \bm{v}^{i} , and use the reward as a signed preference signal for that velocity direction. This gives reward-based velocity matching (RVM), ℒ rvm = 1 2 ​ 𝔼 ​ [ r i ​ ‖ 𝒗 θ ​ ( 𝒙 t i , t ) − 𝒗 i ‖ 2 2 + β ⁡ ( r i ) ​ ‖ 𝒗 θ ​ ( 𝒙 t i , t ) − 𝒗 anc ​ ( 𝒙 t i , t ) ‖ 2 2 ] , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rvm}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\,r^{i}\,\big\|{\bm{v}_{\theta}}(\bm{x}_{t}^{i},t)-\bm{v}^{i}\big\|_{2}^{2}+\beta(r^{i})\,\big\|{\bm{v}_{\theta}}(\bm{x}_{t}^{i},t)-\bm{v}_{\mathrm{anc}}(\bm{x}_{t}^{i},t)\big\|_{2}^{2}\,\Big], where r i r^{i} is a reward-derived weight and 𝒗 anc \bm{v}_{\mathrm{anc}} is an optional anchor velocity. Positive reward weights reinforce the velocity direction associated with a generated sample, while negative weights suppress it. The anchor provides an independent mechanism for controlling model drift and retaining desirable properties of a reference model. Despite its simplicity, RVM generalizes several recent loss functionals, recovering Reinforce Adjoint Matching (RAM) ( Bergmeister et al., 2026 ) and DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al., 2026a ) as special cases under particular choices of reward design and anchor velocity. This unification shifts attention away from the precise algebraic form of the velocity loss and toward the choices that remain: how rewards are transformed into update weights, how the model is anchored, and how samples are generated. We test this view across three generative settings: text-to-image generation with Stable Diffusion 3.5 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , text-to-video generation with Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B ( Team Wan et al., 2025 ) , and image-to-video generation with SkyReels-I2V ( Chen et al., 2025b ) . Across these settings, trajectory-independent velocity-based methods consistently match or outperform trajectory-based baselines. They are also substantially cheaper to train. As demonstrated in Fig. 1 , on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, our RVM recipe uses a 16-step deterministic ODE rollout ( Zhang & Chen, 2023 ; Lu et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023b ) without classifier-free guidance (CFG) and is much efficient, yet achieves higher performance at much lower training cost than trajectory-based methods such as DanceGRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) and FlowGRPO ( Liu et al., 2025b ) . Our experiments on video models further reveal reward design as a key factor. Standard preference and visual-quality rewards can improve even as generated videos become nearly static. To address this failure mode, we introduce a dynamic-tracking (DT) reward based on optical flow that explicitly encourages meaningful motion. Adding DT alone substantially improves VBench Dynamic Degree while also increasing the overall VBench score. These results suggest that reward specification, rather than increasingly elaborate policy-loss design, may be the more influential choices for scalable diffusion-model post-training. Our main contributions are: • We introduce RVM, a simple trajectory-independent method that incorporates reward feedback directly into the native velocity-matching representation of a diffusion model, avoiding policy-ratio estimation and trajectory storage. • We show that RVM provides a general framework that recovers recent methods, including RAM and DiffusionNFT, as special cases. • Through extensive experiments, we show that velocity-based methods can substantially reduce training cost while matching or improving generation quality. Moreover, the differences among velocity-loss variants are relatively small compared with the effects of reward and anchor design. • We extend this framework to large-scale video diffusion models and identify a tendency of generic preference rewards to favor static videos and introduce a dynamic-tracking reward that substantially improves motion while preserving overall video quality. 2 Background 2.1 Diffusion and Flow Models Diffusion and flow-based models ( Song et al., 2020 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Albergo et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) learn a data distribution on ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} by interpolating clean data 𝒙 0 ∼ p data \bm{x}_{0}\sim p_{\rm{data}} and an independent noise ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝑰 ) \bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}) through 𝒙 t = ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝒙 0 + t ​ ϵ \bm{x}_{t}=(1-t)\bm{x}_{0}+t\bm{\epsilon} , or equivalently, 𝒙 t | 𝒙 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝒙 0 , t 2 ​ 𝑰 ) \bm{x}_{t}|\bm{x}_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}((1-t)\bm{x}_{0},t^{2}\bm{I}) . We propose a simple objective for reward fine-tuning of diffusion models that consists of two velocity-regression terms, without using policy ratios or assigning a likelihood interpretation to the loss. The first term performs reward-weighted velocity matching, pulling the predicted velocity toward the velocity directions of high-reward samples. E.3 . 4 Experiments Our experiments address the following two questions: Can reward-based diffusion fine-tuning be simplified to velocity matching without sacrificing performance? And if so, what design choices actually matter? We focus primarily on image and video diffusion models, where each rewarded sample requires an expensive model rollout and training efficiency is particularly desirable. Our main findings are: • In Sec. 4.2 , we compare trajectory-based, ELBO-based, and other recent approaches against our RVM formulation. Our velocity-based approach is comparable or better in both quality and efficiency , achieving comparable or higher reward and benchmark scores with fewer GPU hours. More importantly, we demonstrate that the particular velocity-matching loss forms matter little: RVM, RAM, and DiffusionNFT perform comparably. • In Sec. 4.3 , we isolate the two design choices that remain, (i) the reward and how it is shaped and (ii) the anchoring velocity , and find that the reward function itself is the critical factor . Its choice and the way it is shaped into the per-sample weight account for most of the gain. The choice of anchoring velocity matters in a different way, governing the training dynamics rather than the metrics. Across both T2V and I2V settings, velocity-matching objectives consistently outperform trajectory-based policy-gradient methods. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, RVM achieves the best VBench Overall score of 84.13 84.13 , improving over FlowGRPO ( 75.91 75.91 ), DanceGRPO ( 79.46 79.46 ), and TaRoS-72B ( 80.56 80.56 ). The gain is especially pronounced in motion: RVM reaches a dynamic degree of 75.00 75.00 , compared to 55 55 – 58 58 for trajectory-based methods. A similar trend appears on SkyReels-I2V, where FlowGRPO degrades the base model from 81.68 81.68 to 77.97 77.97 Overall, while RVM reaches 86.27 86.27 . These results suggest that reward-based video diffusion fine-tuning does not require trajectory-level policy-gradient updates to obtain strong performance. The specific velocity-matching objective matters little. On both video diffusion models, DiffusionNFT, RAM, and RVM achieve similar performance across both reward metrics and VBench scores, with differences limited to a few points.
